title: Transesophageal Echocardiography Revealing Mechanical Tricuspid Prosthetic Valve Obstruction with Right-to-Left Shunting Through a Patent Foramen Ovale Causing Refractory Hypoxemia:  A Case Report
content: Mechanical tricuspid prosthetic valve obstruction is a rare but potentially life-threatening complication of prosthetic valve replacement. It typically presents with right-sided heart failure or systemic venous congestion, whereas refractory hypoxemia as the predominant manifestation is uncommon. We report the case of a 34-year-old man who underwent mechanical tricuspid valve replacement 10 years earlier for infective endocarditis, tricuspid valve vegetation, and severe tricuspid regurgitation. He was admitted with sudden-onset dyspnea. Despite endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation with a fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO₂) of 100%, peripheral oxygen saturation remained at 60%–82%, and the arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PaO₂) was 43.7 mmHg. Chest imaging showed no pulmonary parenchymal or vascular abnormalities sufficient to account for the severity of hypoxemia. Transthoracic echocardiography showed abnormal motion of one leaflet of the mechanical tricuspid prosthesis, with a peak transvalvular velocity of 2.6 m/s and a mean transvalvular pressure gradient of 13 mmHg; however, no definite intracardiac right-to-left shunt was identified. Subsequent transesophageal echocardiography showed that the anterior leaflet of the mechanical prosthesis was fixed in a semi-open position and identified an approximately 5-mm communication at the fossa ovalis with marked right-to-left shunting at the atrial level. Emergency surgery revealed extensive thrombus and pannus formation around and beneath the mechanical prosthesis, restricting leaflet motion. Following replacement of the mechanical tricuspid prosthesis with a bioprosthetic valve and closure of the patent foramen ovale, oxygenation rapidly returned to normal. This case suggests that prosthetic valve obstruction associated with intracardiac right-to-left shunting should be considered when severe hypoxemia is disproportionate to pulmonary imaging findings, particularly in the presence of abnormal prosthetic tricuspid leaflet motion or transvalvular hemodynamics. Transesophageal echocardiography permits concurrent assessment of prosthetic valve motion, interatrial septal anatomy, and shunt direction and may provide additional diagnostic information in such complex cases.
